body: There are six public Titles, each awarded to the sole leader in one measure. Hold 3 of them at the start of your own turn and you win at once. A tie awards nothing, and every Title can be taken back: each reads what stands on the board now.
The game runs 14 Years (see Years). If the last one passes before anyone holds 3, the player holding the most Titles wins. Happiness without Calm, then population, then seat order break a tie.
A Title can only be held once its measure passes a floor — set so nothing is winnable at setup or on turn one.

The island is a field of hexes ringed by sea. A land tile prints its terrain and a number of Slots, nothing else. The Slots are one pool: each Building takes one, and each open Slot holds one working Slave, who makes 1 of the terrain's resource. Slaves beyond the open Slots sit idle. Two Colonies on one tile split its Slots, and the Colony founded first takes the odd one.
Hills have no resource: their Slots hold Buildings and their Slaves make nothing, so a Hill City is Freemen, Citizens and Buildings fed from elsewhere.
The single Oracle tile is sacred ground: it can never be settled, by founding, upgrade, or any Event.

Four are drawn from land and Pops: Wood, Stone, Food and Gold. The fifth, Influence, is civic weight. Gold comes from Pops, Trade and Events, never from a tile. No stock goes below zero, except Food during your own turn: a charge takes what you hold and no more. Happiness is not a stock: it is a level read off the board (see Happiness & Unrest).
A Building material, worked from the land by Slaves.
A Building material, worked from the land by Slaves.
Earned by Freemen and Events, and the stock Treasurer counts.
Slaves on Plains grow it. It feeds Freemen and Citizens; end your turn short and one Pop leaves for each missing Food.
Civic weight: spent on demotions, Calm, the Dole, Riot insurance and a second Idea; its great sink is the Assembly.
Every Settlement is worked by three kinds of Pop. Each earns and eats a fixed amount every income, straight from the ruleset:
+1 of the tile's resource for each one on an open Slot

One Pop, one output. A Slave on an open Slot makes the tile's resource and eats nothing; a Freeman makes Gold and eats 1 Food, a Citizen makes Influence and eats 1 Food. Citizens are never grown: every Citizen after setup is a promoted Freeman.

A Settlement holds only so many Pops (see Settlements), and no Building raises the cap. Every way to add a Pop needs room: growing, moving, a Pop Card, the Voyage's settlers, and an Idea or Law grant. Growing, moving and Idea or Law grants count Pops already on their way. There is no penalty for standing over the cap: a Law that cuts capacity only blocks new Pops.
no Buildings but a Port on the coast

You begin with a Capital (a Metropolis of 4 Pops, 1 of them a Citizen) and one founding Colony. Only Cities and the Capital may raise Buildings; in a Colony every Slot is a work Slot, and the one thing it may raise is a Port on the coast.

Your pieces are 4 Colonies and 3 Cities; the Capital is its own piece. Upgrading a Colony hands its piece back, so once every Colony piece stands the way to expand again is to make one of them a City.
Base cost: 4 Wood, 1 Food and a Colony piece — beside an owned Settlement, or on any coastal tile if you hold a coast (sailing, not teleporting). The Pop you send moves free.

Base cost: 3 Wood, 3 Stone and a City piece — lifts the Pop cap, unlocks Building, and returns the Colony piece. Cities never stand side by side, and the new City drives off a rival Colony on its tile.

A turn resolves in order: your Pops on the move arrive, then Victory, then income (every Settlement earns and eats), your drawn Event, your actions, then End Turn. Hunger, then Riots and Revolts, are checked when you end your turn, before it passes.

The verbs are Grow, People (Promote, Demote, move), Expand (found, upgrade), Build, Civic (Calm, the Dole, Ideas, Development Cards) and Trade (offers to the other seats). Anything that targets the map — founding, growing, moving, promoting — is a click on the board itself.

Some actions are throttled so a turn can't do everything at once: one grow per Settlement, one ladder move, one Pop move, one civic Calm, and one Development Card bought and one played per turn. An Idea can be bought once per game. Founding, upgrading and Building are limited by what you can pay and by your pieces.
Grow adds one new Pop to a Settlement with room — once per Settlement per turn. These are base costs; the action picker shows the effective cost under standing Laws.
One ladder move per turn: Promote a Pop up a class, or Demote it down. Promotion buys civic standing; demotion frees labour. The list below shows base costs; the picker shows each effective cost.

One move per turn carries Pops between two of your Settlements for 1 Food a Pop. The target must have room, and they arrive at the start of your next turn. Pops on the move are still in your realm: their Slaves count against your Happiness, and all of them count for your Titles and your Votes.

Cities and the Capital raise Buildings into their Slots, one of each per Settlement. Each Building takes a Slot a Slave could work. A Colony raises nothing but a Port on the coast. Roster prices below are base costs; build controls show effective costs.
Each Slave here makes 2; not on a Hill
Claims one adjacent Luxury good, and keeps it; needs the coast

Each good sits off the shared vertex of two coastal tiles. A Port (base cost 4 Gold, 2 Stone) raised in a Settlement on either tile claims it — a Colony may raise one too. The first Port wins. A good counts only while its holder has a Port beside it, and a second one is a backup. Lose every such Port, to a Riot's fire or a rival's City, and the good goes back to the board unclaimed: the next Port built beside it claims it, yours included, and one already standing does not. A Port needs the coast and a good adjacent, claimed or not; beside a rival's good it lets you take that good in Trade.

Every good you hold adds +2 to your Happiness for as long as you hold it, and there is no limit on how many count. The Riot and Revolt lines and the Beloved of the People laurel both read it. A Blockade Year counts none of them.

subs: After placement, the seats draft one Idea each, in turn, continuing the placement snake. Each pick is public at once, and an Idea belongs to one seat only. Buy a second Idea from the untaken ones during your turn through Civic → Ideas for 6 Influence. Ideas cannot be replaced.
body: Add one Slave or Freeman when taking this Idea
Upgrading adds one Freeman if there is room
Founding grants 1 Slave as room allows
Buy up to 3 Votes per Assembly

Happiness is a level you read off the board, and nothing is saved up. Count +1 for every Temple and +2 for every Luxury, then take 1 for every 2 Slaves in your realm, those on the move included, and 1 for every Unrest Token. Calm bought this Year adds +2, and a standing Law can add a line of its own (Civic Pride, Manumission). If nothing on the board changes, the level is the same next turn.

Unrest Tokens are the one part that stays. Cards and Directives place them: a Happiness loss of any size places one token, and a gain clears one (Festival clears them all). They cannot be bought off. A Riot or a Revolt clears them all.

Hunger is separate. Your Freemen and Citizens eat at income, which can take your Food below zero. You have that turn to buy the Food back. If you end the turn short, one Pop leaves per missing Food and Food returns to zero, before the Riot check. You choose which Freemen or Citizens leave; Freemen are picked first unless you change it.

One civic Calm per turn, both worth +2 Happiness this Year. It expires when the Year turns and does not count toward Beloved of the People. These are base costs; the payment picker shows effective costs:

At a level of -3 or below when you end your turn, your Unrest Tokens clear and a Riot rolls before the turn passes. Declare insurance first (each once, +1 to the roll); the concession demotes a Citizen. Pop losses take Slaves first, then Freemen, then Citizens, and for each one you may discard a held Development Card, drawn at random, instead. At -6 or below it is a Revolt instead: half your Slaves leave, rounded down, your tokens clear, and nothing is rolled.
The Agora fills with angry voices. Declare your concessions before the dice decide.

A Year is one turn for every seat. As each Year opens, the top Card of the Year deck is turned up and stands for that Year; the next Card stays hidden. The seat that plays first moves on one place each Year.
The game runs 14 Years and the deck holds 14 Cards; a longer game shuffles the spent Cards back in. After the last Year the age ends.

Most Year Cards strike out one term for every realm for the whole Year, a class Building's raise included. Plague and Festival act once, on everyone, when they are turned up. The player deck (40 Cards) deals you a private Card each income.

Free Settlers and Captured Laborers offer a Pop: take it in a Settlement with room, or decline. A declined Card goes to the bottom of the player deck and gives nothing, and the table sees which Card it was. With no room anywhere, the Card is discarded.
Plains grow no Food this Year.
Forests yield no Wood this Year.
Mountains yield no Stone this Year.
Freemen yield no Gold this Year.
Citizens yield no Influence this Year.
Luxuries give no Happiness this Year.
Gain a Freeman in a Settlement with room. You may decline it: it goes to the bottom of the deck.
Gain a Slave in a Settlement with room. You may decline it: it goes to the bottom of the deck.

On your turn, once your Event Card is resolved, the Trade disc opens an offer. Wood, Stone, Food, Gold, Influence, claimed Luxury goods and Pops all Trade; Votes, Ideas, Laws, Settlements and Buildings never do.

An offer goes to the table, or only to the seats you pick. Every seat sees it, and the seats it names accept, decline or counter. Each side gives at least one thing, at any ratio, and only what it holds.

The first seat to accept trades, at once; both sides are checked again as it settles. A counter waits for you to take it, and dies with the offer if another seat accepts first. You may withdraw an offer, and your open offers close when your turn ends.

A Luxury good carries its +2 Happiness to its new holder. Pops leave at once, travel like a move to a Settlement with room picked on the map, and arrive at the start of their new owner’s next turn; from the Trade on they are its Pops.
There is no Bank. Trade is the only way to turn one stock into another, apart from the Dole, where 3 Influence buys 1 Food. Nothing anchors a price: a deal is whatever two seats agree.
Until every seat presses Ready, any seat may offer and answer. A Ready seat makes no new offers. When the last seat is Ready, open offers close and the ballots begin.
Once a turn, after your Event Card, pay 2 Gold and draw the top Development Card. One deck of 40 serves the table; when it runs out, the discards are shuffled into a new pile.

A yield resolves the moment it is drawn: the table sees it, you take what it gives, and it goes to the discards. Your Settlements are your Capital, Cities and Colonies; your Pops are every Slave, Freeman and Citizen, those on the move included.

Every other Development Card goes into your hand, face down. Everyone sees how many each seat holds, never which. On your turn you may play one you did not draw this turn. It resolves at once and goes to the discards, face up.

Raiders, Agitators and an Informer name a rival when you play them, and cannot take what that rival does not have: Raiders names a stock the rival holds, and an Informer needs a rival who holds a Development Card.

At the end of your own turn, at the Riot check, a Happiness level of +3 or higher draws one Card free. Calm does not count, the level is read after Hunger, and there is no Food condition. A yield lands at once; a held Card is playable from your next turn. With the pile and the discards empty, nothing is drawn.

When a Riot takes Pops, you answer each one: lose the Pop, or discard a held Card drawn at random. You choose before the Card is drawn. It is a discard, not your Card for the turn. Buildings and stocks go as the row says, and a Revolt still costs its Slaves.
Yield, on the draw. Gain 1 Food for each of your Settlements.
Yield, on the draw. Gain 1 Wood for each of your Settlements.
Yield, on the draw. Gain 1 Stone for each of your Settlements.
Yield, on the draw. Gain 1 Food for each Pop in your realm.
Yield, on the draw. Gain 1 Influence for each Pop in your realm.
Yield, on the draw. Gain 5 Food.
Yield, on the draw. Gain 5 Wood.
Yield, on the draw. Gain 5 Stone.
Held. Gain 1 Wood, Stone or Food for each of your Settlements: one kind, chosen when you play it.
Held. Gain a Freeman in one of your Settlements with room.
Held. Gain a Slave in one of your Settlements with room.
Held. Your next Building or Colony upgrade this turn costs 2 less Wood or Stone: one kind, chosen when you play it.
Held. Clear one of your Unrest Tokens.
Held, played on a rival. Take up to 3 Wood, Stone, Food or Gold from a rival you pick: one kind, and no more than they hold.
Held, played on a rival. A rival you pick places an Unrest Token.
Held, played on a rival. A rival you pick discards a held Card, drawn at random.
The Assembly meets every other Year from Year 2, before the Year's opener takes their turn. Nothing else happens while it sits — the whole table proposes and Votes, then play resumes.

This is what Influence is for. Everything the Assembly asks of you to draw or Repeal is paid in Influence. Extra Votes take Gold or Influence. Participation prices in this reference are base costs; Assembly controls show effective costs.
Every player decides independently and in secret whether to propose one Resolution or pass. There is no house Resolution.
Pay 2 Influence to draw from a Politician you choose. The Politician is your pick; the Resolution is not. You see it in secret.
You may propose your draw or discard it and pass. No redraw.
Seal the Resolution for the ballot. A Stratokles Directive must name one rival; both the Directive and its target are revealed before voting. One proposal per player per Assembly.

A Law that would replace a protected Law is blocked, but you may still seal it. It is checked again at its turn on the ballot: if it is still blocked, it is not voted and you keep it. Everyone sees it. At the next sitting propose it with no draw, or draw a new Card; drawing, a Repeal or a pass sends it to the discards.
For 3 Influence, move to strike a standing Law whose protection has ended, instead. It is voted like any other Resolution — undoing a Law is as political as passing one.
Say nothing. Always available, whatever your Influence.
The ballot is voted one Resolution at a time, repeals first, then the rest in turn order, openly — every Vote is visible as it lands, so the last seat to speak on a close Vote is a kingmaker.
One seat Vote plus one per Citizen. Rural Bloc changes Settlement Votes. Isonomia fixes its target’s base at one.
More yea than nay carries. A tie fails.

2 Gold or Influence buys one extra Vote, up to 2 per player per Assembly, bought on your turn to cast. They count on every ballot left in the sitting. The cap is what stops a hoard from simply buying the outcome.

A Resolution is not a one-Year buff — it changes how the game is played. Three of the four Politicians deal in Laws: table-wide rules that stand until repealed, each with a downside, so a Vote is a referendum on which strategy the table backs.
The other, Stratokles, deals in Directives: one-time upheavals aimed at a rival chosen by their author. Each leaves a permanent monument on his stack.

4 Laws may stand at once. At the cap, a passed Law automatically replaces the oldest. A new price Law also replaces the standing price Law; the price Laws are Sacred Fields, Manumission, Tenant Rights, Festival Calendar, Public Works, Colonial Charter, Harbour Dues. Stratokles's monuments take no Slot — they are not rules.
A Law already standing cannot be enacted again.
A new Law is protected through the following sitting, including against replacement and The Stele Is Broken. Capacity or Slot cuts keep existing Pops and Buildings.
A player whose Resolution passes immediately receives that Politician's prize. Failed Votes and Repeal motions pay nothing.
A Politician's power is the number of their Stelae standing; their Patron is whoever authored the most of them. A tie leaves them unpatroned. Patron is descriptive only and grants no buff.
Held by whoever authored the most standing Laws, with at least 2. A tie awards it to nobody. A Repeal or a replaced Law takes one off its author, and a Directive never counts.
Food, labour and the social ladder.
Slaves grow Food on any terrain, but Estates may not be built.
Temples also grow 2 Food, but cost 6 Stone.
Promoting a Slave is free, but Slaves count twice for Unrest.
Growing a Slave costs 2 Gold; growing a Freeman costs 3 Gold.
Freemen eat no Food, but Marketplaces do nothing.
Civic Calm costs 2 Food or 2 Influence.
Estates and Granaries cost 3 Wood; Marketplaces cost 2 Wood and 2 Gold. Colonies hold 3 Pops.
Your Capital may grow twice per turn, but Colonies may not grow.
Citizens in Colonies make 2 Influence; Freemen in Colonies make 0 Gold.
Your realm gains 1 Happiness, but each City pays 1 Gold a Year.
Cities gain one Building Slot, but you may place one fewer Colony piece.
Colonies, their Buildings and their Votes.
Colonies may hold one Building, but Cities lose one Slot.
Founding a Colony costs 1 Food and a Pop; upgrading one costs 6 Stone.
Founding a Colony grants a free Slave, but Colonies hold 3 Pops.
Ports cost 2 Stone; Marketplaces cost 3 Wood and 4 Gold.
Each Colony casts one Vote, but each City casts one fewer.
Choose a rival. They lose 3 Food.
Choose a rival. They place an Unrest Token.
Choose a rival. They collect no income next turn.
Choose a rival. They lose a Pop from their largest Settlement.
Choose a rival. Their newest authored Law is repealed if its minimum tenure has ended.
Choose a rival. They have one base Vote at the next Assembly.
